papers.title_in_file: Optimal Stratification of a Sampling Frame: A Comparative Study of Classical, Quantum, and Quantum-Inspired Approaches
papers.version_note: arXiv:2608.10787v1 [stat.ME], 11 Aug 2026; the text is the paper its record names.
papers.what_it_is: A case study that runs one 20-stratum survey-stratification QUBO surrogate on a simulated-annealing stand-in for D-Wave, IBM QAOA, QCi Dirac-3 and a GPU Ising machine, and compares each with a classical genetic algorithm that optimises the Bethel sample size directly.

existing.note: The numbers are right. Section 6.1 limits the reading of 'genuine optimisation': the authors say the device's native energy scale is not documented well enough to certify from it alone that the search was effective, as opposed to merely well-behaved. The 100-variable free-tier cap is stated in Section 5.1, and the 160 and 129 figures are the best-known results, not certified optima.
existing.value: The authors report that on the twenty-stratum frame, under the free-tier cap of one hundred decision variables, the QCi Dirac-3 partition has a Bethel sample size of 286, against 160 for the best-known QUBO solution (Fixstars Amplify AE, a GPU Ising machine) and 129 for the SamplingStrata genetic algorithm; re-evaluated under the common one-hot objective its energy is 936.61 against the best-known 501.0. The authors say the Dirac-3 run shows evidence of a non-trivial optimisation process, but that its native energy scale is not documented well enough to certify from it alone that the underlying search was effective.
existing.anchor: Section 6, p.16; Section 6.1, pp.17-18; Section 5.1, p.15
quotes: QAOA returns 262 and the QCi Dirac-3 returns 286.
achieves a total sample size of 129
reaches an objective value of 501.0 in about five seconds, giving a sample size of 160

Reevaluating the decoded Dirac-3 partition directly under the identical common one-hot objective (same weights, same penalty) used for D-Wave and Amplify AE gives an energy of 936.61, against the best-known 501.0
On the QCi Dirac-3 the free tier caps a degree-two problem at one hundred decision variables.
the native energy scale is not documented well enough, however, to certify from it alone that the underlying search was effective, as opposed to merely well-behaved.
existing.certainty_reason: One preprint case study, on a single 20-stratum instance, under heterogeneous free-tier budgets that the authors say make it a case study and not a controlled experiment.
existing.reader_inference: The 286 against 160 comparison isolates the device, because 160 is already the surrogate's best-known Bethel value; the 160 against 129 part is the formulation's share. The paper does not compare the Dirac-3 run to a random baseline, as it does for IBM.

assertions.value: The authors state that the analysis is restricted to the 589 municipalities of a single region of the swissmunicipalities dataset, and that on the actual data twenty of the possible atomic strata are non-empty, four of which are singletons.
quotes: The analysis is restricted to the 589 municipalities of a single region
on the actual data twenty of these are non-empty, four of which are singletons.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own data and frame in Section 5.

assertions.value: The authors state that the precision requirement is a coefficient of variation of five percent on each target variable and that the aggregation target is K = 4 final strata.
quotes: The precision requirement is a coefficient of variation of five percent on each target variable, and the aggregation target is K = 4 final strata.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own setup in Section 5.

assertions.value: The authors state that the four solvers differ in hardware, computational budget, iteration count and, for IBM, the encoding itself, so the comparison is a case study and not a fully controlled experiment.
quotes: The solvers differ not only in hardware but also in computational budget, iteration count and, for IBM, the encoding itself, so the comparison isolates a case study rather than a fully controlled experiment.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of the scope of their comparison, in the abstract and again in Sections 1 and 5.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that the choice of a twenty-stratum frame is operational, not statistical: it is the largest problem that all three quantum platforms can accept on their freely available tiers.
quotes: The choice of a twenty-stratum frame is not statistical but operational: it is the largest problem that all three quantum platforms can accept on their freely available tiers
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of why the instance is this small.
assertions.reader_inference: The result says nothing about larger frames, where the paper itself expects the IBM circuit depth to grow.

assertions.value: The authors report that the SamplingStrata genetic algorithm, operating directly on the atomic strata, achieves a total sample size of 129, and say this figure is the best-known result obtained, not a certified optimum, because restart and seed distributions were not systematically logged.
quotes: achieves a total sample size of 129
the genetic algorithm is stochastic, and this figure should be read as the best-known result obtained rather than a certified optimum
assertions.certainty_reason: A single-instance empirical result from a stochastic search, with the authors' own caveat that it is not a certified optimum.

assertions.value: The authors report that an optimised Bethel allocation applied to all twenty atomic strata without clustering requires 105, and that the KmeansSolution routine, used as a reference initialisation and not as a competing solver, requires 312.
quotes: strata without any clustering step, requires 105; because the starting frame is already coarse, aggregating to four strata sacrifices some efficiency
The KmeansSolution routine requires 312
assertions.certainty_reason: Single-instance computed values reported by one preprint.

assertions.value: The authors report that the Fixstars Amplify AE GPU Ising machine reaches an objective value of 501.0 in about five seconds, giving a sample size of 160, and that an independent, more thorough simulated-annealing search converges repeatedly on the same value, so 501.0 is treated as the best-known solution of this QUBO without a certificate of global optimality.
quotes: reaches an objective value of 501.0 in about five seconds, giving a sample size of 160

an independent, more thorough simulated-annealing search run as a check converges repeatedly on that same value, so 501.0 is treated throughout as the best-known solution of this QUBO, though without a certificate of global optimality
assertions.certainty_reason: A single-instance empirical result; the authors state it is not certified optimal.

assertions.value: The authors report that a short best-of-ten classical simulated-annealing run of the D-Wave formulation settles on a weaker local optimum, implying an objective of about 566.0, and a sample size of 162. They state that the QPU and hybrid modes were not accessible on the available plan, so no D-Wave quantum hardware result is reported.
quotes: settles instead on a visibly weaker local optimum, implying an objective of about 566.0, and correspondingly returns a sample size of 162
In this study the QPU/hybrid modes were not accessible on the available plan, and the QUBO was solved with classical simulated annealing
assertions.certainty_reason: Single-instance result of a classical run; the paper's own statement of what was and was not run.
assertions.reader_inference: Any reading of the 'D-Wave' row of Table 3 as a quantum-annealer result is wrong: it is classical simulated annealing.

assertions.value: The authors report that IBM QAOA returned a sample size of 262 from a severely truncated proof-of-execution run of only two COBYLA iterations, with a transpiled circuit of depth roughly 4,900 and about 5,300 two-qubit gates. They state it is not a general measurement of QAOA performance.
quotes: QAOA returns 262 and the QCi Dirac-3 returns 286.
With only two COBYLA iterations, imposed by the free-tier time budget, this is a severely truncated proof-of-execution run on real IBM
a circuit of depth roughly 4,900 with about 5,300 two-qubit gates
assertions.certainty_reason: A single truncated hardware run, as the authors describe it.

assertions.value: The authors report that 10,000 uniformly random four-cluster assignments of the same twenty atomic strata, evaluated with the same Bethel-Chromy allocator, have sample sizes with a median of 314 and a range from 162 to 383, and that IBM's value lies at approximately the 12th percentile of that distribution. They say the IBM run performed essentially no optimisation.
quotes: 10,000 uniformly random four-cluster assignments of the same twenty atomic strata were generated
the resulting sample sizes have a median of 314 and range from 162 to 383
lies at approximately the 12th percentile of this distribution of individual random assignments
assertions.certainty_reason: A simulated random baseline on one instance; the authors note that the number of distinct bitstrings sampled was not recorded, so a matched best-of-m comparison could not be built.
assertions.reader_inference: IBM's 262 sits better than the typical random partition only because it is the lowest-cost of a handful of sampled bitstrings; the paper says as much and does not claim QAOA structure.

assertions.value: The authors state that the evidence the IBM run failed to optimise lies in the absence of any energy improvement across the two iterations and in the diffuse, non-repeating bitstring distribution, and that no separate check against an ideal or lightly-noised simulator was performed to isolate noise from other causes.
quotes: the diagnostic evidence that the run failed to optimise lies instead in the absence of any energy improvement across the two iterations
No separate check against an ideal or lightly-noised simulator was performed for this specific run to isolate the two.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of the IBM diagnosis in Section 6.1.
assertions.reader_inference: The attribution of the IBM shortfall to SWAP-routing depth is therefore an inference, not an isolated cause.

assertions.value: The authors state that the IBM run used the ibm_kingston backend (Heron r2, 156 qubits), and that the QAOA layer count p and the number of shots per circuit evaluation were not recorded in a reportable form.
quotes: The real hardware run used the ibm_kingston backend (Heron r2, 156 qubits)
The exact QAOA layer count p and the number of shots per circuit evaluation were not recorded in a form that can be reported precisely here
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this reproducibility gap in Appendix A.5.

assertions.value: The authors state that the IBM implementation does not use the one-hot encoding but assigns each atomic stratum a binary label of ceil(log2 K) qubits, so L atomic strata need L times that many qubits, giving forty qubits for the twenty-stratum problem at K = 4, and that the Hamiltonian therefore encodes the same dispersion criterion by a different polynomial, so raw IBM energies are not compared with the one-hot energies.
quotes: so a problem with L atomic strata requires Lb qubits; for K = 4, two qubits per stratum give forty qubits for the twenty-stratum problem.
which is why the two solvers’ raw Hamiltonian energies are not compared directly anywhere in this paper
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors define the IBM encoding in Section 4.6.

assertions.value: The authors report that the Dirac-3 returned ten distinct low-energy solutions with only a single, easily repaired constraint violation, and that its final native energy was clearly negative.
quotes: it returned ten distinct low-energy solutions with only a single, easily repaired constraint violation
its final native energy, as reported by the device, was clearly negative
assertions.certainty_reason: A single-run empirical observation reported by the authors.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors offer this as evidence of a non-trivial optimisation, but they also say the native scale cannot certify it; the common-objective energy of 936.61 is the quantity they rely on.

assertions.value: The authors state that no linear relationship between the Dirac-3's native energy and the common one-hot QUBO energy is documented by the vendor or established in the study, so the two scales are not compared directly and every Dirac-3 comparison uses the common QUBO energy or the downstream Bethel sample size.
quotes: is documented by the vendor or established in this study; the two scales are therefore not compared directly anywhere in this paper
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of the Dirac-3 comparison in Section 6.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Dirac-3's underlying physical mechanism was not independently verified in the study and is reported as described by the provider.
quotes: The underlying physical mechanism was not independently verified in this study and is therefore reported as described by the provider.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of what they did not verify.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Dirac-3 free tier caps a degree-two problem at one hundred decision variables, and that the one-hot QUBO needs L times K variables, so the ceiling would be reached at L = 25 atomic strata at K = 4; twenty strata (eighty variables) were accepted and the boundary was not tested directly.
quotes: so at K = 4 the ceiling of one hundred variables would be reached at L = 25 atomic strata under this reading
though this was not tested directly at the boundary
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the quota that bounds the instance size.

assertions.value: The authors state that an initially considered Dirac-3 qudit formulation with squared label differences was inappropriate for nominal cluster labels, because it introduces an artificial ordering and, with non-negative weights, is minimised by giving every atomic stratum the same label; the study therefore uses the one-hot QUBO.
quotes: it introduces an artificial ordering
is minimised by assigning every atomic stratum the same label, the degenerate single-cluster solution
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state which formulation they rejected and why, which bounds what the Dirac-3 result covers.

assertions.value: The authors report that QCi documentation is inconsistent on the Dirac-3 total qudit-level capacity: the Developer Beginner Guide states 949 while the eqc-direct integer-solver documentation states 954, and the paper adopts 954, which with two levels per binary variable gives roughly 119 atomic strata at K = 4 under full paid access.
quotes: the Dirac-3 Developer Beginner Guide states 949, while the eqc-direct integer-solver documentation states 954
so full access would accommodate roughly 119 atomic strata at K = 4
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's description of its own product, reported second-hand with a stated discrepancy between two vendor sources.

assertions.value: The authors define the surrogate as a population-weighted pairwise within-cluster dispersion: plain Euclidean distance between standardised mean and standard-deviation feature vectors, scaled by the square root of the product of the two strata's populations. They state this is a design choice and that its relationship to the squared-distance pairwise identity is heuristic, not derived.
quotes: plain Euclidean distance scaled by the square root of the product of populations, is a design choice for the surrogate
the relationship between them is heuristic rather than derived
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors define their own surrogate in Section 4.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Bethel objective has no direct QUBO representation, and that dropping the factor 1/(2 N_k) from the pairwise identity to obtain a valid QUBO changes the criterion and can alter the ranking of partitions, especially when final-stratum sizes differ substantially.
quotes: dropping the factor 1/{2Nk(z)} to obtain a valid QUBO changes the criterion and can alter the ranking of partitions
so CB(z) has no direct QUBO representation
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of the formulation in Section 4.3 and Appendix A.3; no formal theorem is stated.
assertions.reader_inference: This is the paper's stated reason why every QUBO route minimises a proxy; it is argued from the form of the objective, not proved as a numbered theorem.

assertions.value: The authors report that the one-hot penalty weight lambda was set to three times the largest pairwise weight, 476.92, while the sufficient condition for no profitable violation is a weight above the largest total pairwise weight incident on one stratum, 1,729.23, which the weight used does not meet; decoded solutions were checked and repaired for one-hot violations instead.
quotes: Throughout this study λ = 3 maxh,h′ whh′ = 476.92
For the twenty-stratum case study this quantity is 1,729.23, so the penalty actually used does not meet this sufficient condition
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' statement of their own parameter choice and its consequence.
assertions.reader_inference: Because the penalty can be violated, the reported energies and sample sizes depend on the repair rule; a Dirac-3 or D-Wave raw bitstring is not the object that was scored.

assertions.value: The authors state that every decoded solution was repaired by a stated rule when it violated the one-hot constraint or left a cluster empty, that energies and sample sizes were recomputed on the repaired partition, and that all solver results in Table 3 and Figure 5 were feasible after repair with exactly four non-empty final strata.
quotes: The common QUBO energy and the downstream Bethel sample size are always recomputed on the repaired, feasible partition, never on the raw decoded bits.
All solver results reported in Table 3 and Figure 5 were feasible after repair and contained exactly four non-empty final strata.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' statement of their own evaluation procedure.

assertions.value: The authors state that every reported sample size is the sum of component-wise ceilings of the continuous Bethel-Chromy allocation, which is feasible but not guaranteed to be the smallest integer allocation meeting the precision constraints, and that all methods are scored by this same reported quantity.
quotes: is feasible but not guaranteed to be the smallest integer allocation meeting the precision constraints
Every method compared in this study is scored by the same CBreported, so the comparison between methods remains valid
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors define the evaluated quantity in Section 2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the SamplingStrata genetic algorithm evaluates the true objective, the Bethel sample size, at every fitness evaluation, rather than a surrogate.
quotes: the genetic algorithm evaluates the true objective, the Bethel sample size, at every fitness evaluation, rather than a surrogate
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' description of the benchmark method in Section 3.

assertions.value: The authors state that Amplify AE was given the same one-hot encoding, weighted objective and penalty weight but expresses the one-hot condition as a native constraint, so it is not literally handed the same penalised polynomial and a shortfall there cannot rule out algorithmic or computational limits other than quantum-hardware effects.
quotes: the two representations are equivalent on the feasible set, but the solver is not literally handed the same penalised polynomial
it cannot rule out other algorithmic or computational limitations
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of the classical control in Section 4.8.

assertions.value: The authors report that the best-known QUBO solution maps to a sample size of 160 against the genetic-algorithm benchmark of 129, a downstream gap of about twenty-four percent attributed to the formulation. They say this is the best Bethel value associated with the surrogate's best-known solution, not a proven lower bound, and that the gap is consistent with a substantial formulation component although residual heuristic error cannot be excluded.
quotes: This best-known solution corresponds to a sample size of 160, against the classical benchmark of 129
so the formulation is associated with a downstream gap of about twenty-four percent in this instance
this observed gap is consistent with a substantial formulation component, although residual heuristic error cannot be excluded.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical decomposition from one instance; the authors say it is empirical and not certified.
assertions.reader_inference: The 24 percent compares 160 with 129; 160 is the best Bethel value found for the surrogate's best QUBO energy, so the formulation share is that gap, and the device share is each device's distance from 160.

assertions.value: The authors state that no solver in the study, quantum or classical, found a Bethel value below roughly 160 while minimising the surrogate, and say this is empirical evidence and not a mathematical guarantee that none could.
quotes: no solver in this study, quantum or classical, found a Bethel value below roughly 160 while minimising the surrogate
this is empirical evidence rather than a mathematical guarantee that none could
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical observation over a handful of runs on one instance.

assertions.value: The authors state that the surrogate and the Bethel objective are not guaranteed to rank partitions in the same order or share the same minimiser, and that omitting assignment-dependent normalisation terms can favour partitions that are homogeneous under the pairwise criterion but inefficient under the sample-allocation problem.
quotes: the surrogate and the Bethel objective are not guaranteed to rank candidate partitions in the same order or to share the same minimiser
can favour partitions that are homogeneous according to the pairwise criterion but inefficient under the subsequent sample-allocation problem
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' argument, supported by one instance and not proved.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that improving the hardware alone is not sufficient, and that before quantum optimisation can be competitive for optimal stratification the encoded objective must reproduce more closely the ranking induced by the Bethel-Chromy allocation.
quotes: The main methodological implication is therefore that improving the hardware alone is not sufficient.
the objective encoded in the solver must reproduce more closely the ranking induced by the Bethel–Chromy allocation
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusion from one case study.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that, at the scale tested, a classical genetic algorithm remains the method of choice for optimal stratification, and that the findings are empirical and do not establish global optimality for either the genetic-algorithm result or the QUBO solutions.
quotes: The paper concludes that, at the scale tested, a classical genetic algorithm remains the method of choice for optimal stratification.
These findings are empirical and do not establish global optimality for either the genetic-algorithm result or the QUBO solutions.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' conclusion from one 20-stratum case study.

assertions.value: The authors state that no embedding of the actual, sparser clustering QUBO graph was computed, and that the documented complete-graph embedding capacity on Pegasus is about 150 variables with perfect yield, degrading in practice beyond roughly 120 owing to broken chains; applied to the one-hot QUBO this gives an illustrative, conservative reference of roughly thirty to thirty-seven atomic strata with four final strata.
quotes: No embedding of this actual, sparser graph was computed in this study.
about 150 variables with perfect yield, degrading in practice beyond roughly 120 owing to broken chains
roughly thirty to thirty-seven
assertions.certainty_reason: A documented capacity figure taken from other sources, applied by the authors as a conservative estimate; no embedding was run.

assertions.value: The authors argue that paid IBM access would remove the time and session limits that cut the loop to two COBYLA iterations but not the binding physical constraint of circuit depth, since the transpiled circuit has roughly five thousand two-qubit gates, and that error mitigation extends usable depth at exponentially growing sampling cost.
quotes: It would not, however, remove the binding constraint, because that constraint is physical rather than contractual
Error mitigation extends the usable depth but at exponentially growing sampling cost
assertions.certainty_reason: A prediction by the authors, not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors report that transpiling the identical QAOA circuit at K = 4 inflates the two-qubit gate count from 1,900 on an all-to-all coupling map to 5,354 on a heavy-hex map, matching the 5,354 two-qubit gates measured on the real IBM run, and that at K = 2 the count more than doubles, from 380 to 834.
quotes: At K = 4, routing inflates the gate count from 1,900 (all-to-all) to 5,354 (heavy-hex)
at K = 2 the same effect more than doubles the gate count (380 to 834)
assertions.certainty_reason: An offline compilation count from one circuit with the standard Qiskit transpiler.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's text states 5,354 as the measured count on the real run, while Section 6.1 says about 5,300; the two are consistent.

assertions.value: The authors report that a heuristic signal-survival indicator, two-qubit gate fidelity raised to the number of gates, falls to well under 0.1% on heavy-hex at both K values, against about 15% at K = 4 and about two-thirds at K = 2 for all-to-all connectivity, using representative fidelities for superconducting and trapped-ion hardware. They say the indicator is a simplified proxy, not a computed success probability, and that it supports without proving the connectivity-based explanation of the IBM failure.
quotes: falls to well under 0.1% at both K values
about 15% at K = 4, and about two-thirds at K = 2
This supports, without by itself proving, the connectivity-based explanation of the IBM failure
assertions.certainty_reason: A heuristic proxy computed from gate counts; not a measured or simulated success probability.

assertions.value: The authors recommend recompiling the same logical Hamiltonian and ansatz for a fully connected coupling map on a trapped-ion device (IonQ Forte or Quantinuum H2/Helios), starting with the cheaper K = 2 case as a minimal-cost first test of the connectivity hypothesis, and state that this would not change the conclusion about the formulation.
quotes: starting with the cheaper K = 2 case as a minimalcost first test of the connectivity hypothesis before attempting the full K = 4 problem
This would not, however, change the conclusion regarding the formulation established in Section 6.2
assertions.certainty_reason: A proposed future experiment; no trapped-ion run was made.
assertions.reader_inference: No trapped-ion result is reported, so nothing in this paper bears on whether all-to-all gate-based hardware would do better.

assertions.value: The authors list possible directions for bringing the optimisation closer to the Bethel objective: constructing local quadratic approximations from classical Bethel evaluations, using constrained or nonlinear hybrid models, or introducing auxiliary variables to approximate assignment-dependent quantities, and say each option increases the variable count, the approximation error or the surrounding classical computation.
quotes: Possible directions include constructing local quadratic approximations from classical Bethel evaluations, using constrained or nonlinear hybrid models, or introducing auxiliary variables to approximate assignment-dependent quantities.
Each option increases either the number of variables, the approximation error, or the amount of classical computation surrounding the quantum solver.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this open problem in Section 6.3.

assertions.value: The authors state that artificial intelligence tools, including ChatGPT and Claude, were used to generate the code and improve the language of the paper, that all outputs were reviewed by the authors, and that the code and data are available in a public repository.
quotes: were used to generate the code and improve language, readability, and clarity of the paper.
The data and software required to reproduce the computational workflow are available at https://github.com/barcaroli/QuantumComputing.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own disclosure statements on the first page.
